Computer Science Labs

Image Processing · Lab 14 · Material

Composing and Auditing Policies

MaterialPracticeQuiz

Combine familiar image operations into policies you can inspect and replay. You will also build mixed images with targets that match their actual construction.

What you will learn

  • Explain why operation order and repeated resampling matter.
  • Audit sampled probabilities, ranges and severity budgets.
  • Construct MixUp and CutMix images with consistent soft targets.
  • Prepare a controlled policy comparison without inventing model results.

Before this lab: Use bounded geometric and photometric augmentation, class one-hot vectors and reproducible generators.

In this lab

  1. Operation Order
  2. Affine Composition and One Resampling
  3. Severity Budgets
  4. Auditing Sampled Distributions
  5. MixUp Images and Soft Targets
  6. CutMix and Actual Clipped Area
  7. Batch Pairing and Target Bookkeeping
  8. Controlled Policy Comparison Plans

Prepare your notebook

Use a Python notebook with OpenCV, Pillow, NumPy and Matplotlib. Run the setup once, then run the guided blocks in order. The copy button selects only the code.

The examples were checked with OpenCV 4.13, Pillow 12.3, NumPy 2.2 and Matplotlib 3.11. The repository’s Python requirements list the versions. These pages and images open offline; running the code requires the Python libraries.

Fixtures are RGB uint8, H,W,C. Mixing uses float32 [0,1] arrays and class order [mug, apple]; no model is trained.

Python · shared setup
import json
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path
from io import BytesIO
import numpy as np
import cv2
from PIL import Image, ImageDraw
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
cv2.setNumThreads(1)
rng = np.random.default_rng(214)

# Drawn tabletop fixtures: RGB uint8, H=128, W=160, C=3.
def scene(kind="mug", seed=0):
    local = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    yy, xx = np.mgrid[:128, :160]
    grain = 4 * np.sin(xx / 3) + local.normal(0, 1, (128, 160))
    base = np.stack([205 + yy / 8 + grain, 191 + yy / 10 + grain,
                     166 + yy / 12 + grain], axis=-1)
    canvas = Image.fromarray(np.clip(base, 0, 255).astype(np.uint8))
    draw = ImageDraw.Draw(canvas)
    for y in range(12, 128, 24):
        draw.line((0, y, 159, y), fill=(184, 168, 146), width=1)
    if kind == "mug":
        draw.ellipse((105, 43, 139, 87), fill=(53, 118, 167))
        draw.ellipse((112, 50, 131, 80), fill=(208, 193, 168))
        draw.rounded_rectangle((43, 33, 115, 102), radius=12, fill=(66, 145, 194))
        draw.ellipse((43, 27, 115, 48), fill=(34, 71, 91))
        draw.ellipse((48, 31, 110, 43), fill=(116, 71, 40))
        draw.text((64, 64), "TEA", fill=(245, 246, 237))
    elif kind == "parcel":
        draw.rectangle((27, 31, 123, 101), fill=(174, 117, 65), outline=(70, 45, 28), width=2)
        draw.rectangle((69, 32, 80, 100), fill=(224, 190, 124))
        draw.rectangle((86, 48, 115, 77), fill=(247, 244, 225))
        draw.text((89, 55), "UP", fill=(25, 30, 34))
        draw.line((39, 64, 39, 45), fill=(25, 30, 34), width=3)
        draw.polygon([(33, 48), (45, 48), (39, 41)], fill=(25, 30, 34))
    elif kind == "apple":
        draw.ellipse((43, 38, 115, 108), fill=(190, 48, 40))
        draw.ellipse((58, 44, 75, 63), fill=(241, 123, 93))
        draw.line((80, 42, 86, 26), fill=(75, 63, 32), width=5)
        draw.ellipse((84, 25, 104, 35), fill=(54, 117, 56))
    else:
        raise ValueError("Unknown fixture kind")
    return np.asarray(canvas).copy()

def panels(images, titles, cmap=None):
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(images), figsize=(4 * len(images), 3.4), squeeze=False)
    for ax, image, title in zip(axes[0], images, titles):
        ax.imshow(image, cmap=cmap)
        ax.set_title(title)
        ax.axis("off")
    fig.tight_layout()
    return fig

The image comparisons below come from the guided code. Use their captions and shared display scales to compare each change.

Guided task 01

Operation Order

Two reasonable operations need not commute. Brightness adds an offset, while contrast scales distance from a pivot. Applying contrast after brightness scales the brightness offset too; applying brightness last does not. We use the same source, contrast factor 1.4, pivot 127.5 and offset 25, and delay clipping until the end of each pipeline so the order effect is clear.

A policy record therefore needs an ordered list, not an unordered bag of operation names. Intermediate clipping can introduce another difference by discarding information before later operations run. Make the clipping schedule explicit when comparing implementations. These drawn examples show changes in input evidence, not a ranking of model quality. The right order depends on what appearance variability the task is intended to tolerate and which signals must remain available.

Try it

  1. Convert the mug to float32.
  2. Compute brightness-then-contrast and contrast-then-brightness.
  3. Clip and round only at the end of each chain.
Python · run in order
image = scene("mug")
x = image.astype(np.float32)
bc_raw = 127.5 + 1.4 * ((x+25)-127.5)
cb_raw = 127.5 + 1.4 * (x-127.5) + 25
bc = np.rint(np.clip(bc_raw,0,255)).astype(np.uint8)
cb = np.rint(np.clip(cb_raw,0,255)).astype(np.uint8)
fig = panels([image,bc,cb], ["Original","Brightness then contrast","Contrast then brightness"])

Read the result

Before clipping, the two formulas differ by ten channel levels everywhere. After clipping and rounding, some pixels may differ less. This makes the output behavior understandable from the operations rather than from a vague strength label.

Change and compare

  • Verify the unclipped difference algebraically and numerically.
  • Introduce intermediate clipping and inspect which regions acquire an additional difference.

Guided task 02

Affine Composition and One Resampling

Compose affine maps before resampling when the intended geometry permits it. Homogeneous 3-by-3 matrices make the order explicit: if rotation R happens first and translation T second, the forward map is T@R for column-coordinate vectors. Multiplication order matters. OpenCV accepts the top two rows of the composed matrix for warpAffine.

Compare one composed warp with two successive warps, using a 9.4-pixel translation so both stages involve interpolation. Even when the continuous geometry agrees, two resamplings can soften details and treat intermediate borders differently. The intermediate canvas may discard pixels that the second operation could otherwise have used. A numeric difference between these paths is therefore expected and is not proof that either library call failed. Prefer a documented single-resampling implementation when it matches the intended transformation; retain separate stages when their intermediate effects are intentional.

Try it

  1. Build a 7-degree rotation and a 9.4-pixel right translation.
  2. Compose T@R in homogeneous coordinates.
  3. Compare one warp with two successive warps.
Python · run in order
h,w = image.shape[:2]
rotation = cv2.getRotationMatrix2D(((w-1)/2,(h-1)/2),7,1)
R = np.vstack([rotation,[0,0,1]])
T = np.array([[1,0,9.4],[0,1,0],[0,0,1]],float)
combined = T @ R
one_warp = cv2.warpAffine(image,combined[:2],(w,h),flags=cv2.INTER_LINEAR,borderValue=(225,218,200))
intermediate = cv2.warpAffine(image,rotation,(w,h),flags=cv2.INTER_LINEAR,borderValue=(225,218,200))
two_warps = cv2.warpAffine(intermediate,T[:2],(w,h),flags=cv2.INTER_LINEAR,borderValue=(225,218,200))
fig = panels([image,one_warp,two_warps], ["Original","Composed: one resampling","Sequential: two resamplings"])

Read the result

Inspect the rim and letters as well as the image border. Geometry can agree while sampled pixels differ. An exact coordinate probe is a better test of matrix order than expecting two differently resampled arrays to be identical.

Change and compare

  • Apply both matrix formulas to one coordinate to verify order.
  • Replace the second transform with an integer translation and compare the interior resampling effect.

Guided task 03

Severity Budgets

A collection of individually modest operations can become excessive when every operation is always applied. A simple budget limits how many different operations are selected for one view. It does not prove semantic safety, but it makes the policy easier to inspect. Here the available operations are horizontal reflection, an 8-degree rotation and a brightness offset of −18, with at most two distinct operations per view.

Sample operation indices without replacement, then sort them to enforce the documented order flip, rotate, brightness. Selection randomness and execution order are separate decisions. A budget of zero produces a copy of the original; a budget of two does not mean twice the visual severity of a budget of one. The operations affect different properties. Use the recorded names to explain each result and review whether combinations remove evidence required by the label.

Try it

  1. Define the fixed operation order.
  2. Select distinct operations without replacement using seed 914.
  3. Generate views with budgets zero, one and two.
Python · run in order
operation_names = ["flip","rotate","brightness"]
budget_rng = np.random.default_rng(914)
budget_views, selected_records = [],[]
for budget in [0,1,2]:
    selected = sorted(budget_rng.choice(3,size=budget,replace=False).tolist())
    view = image.copy()
    for index in selected:
        if index == 0:
            view = view[:,::-1].copy()
        elif index == 1:
            affine = cv2.getRotationMatrix2D(((w-1)/2,(h-1)/2),8,1)
            view = cv2.warpAffine(view,affine,(w,h),borderValue=(225,218,200))
        else:
            view = np.rint(np.clip(view.astype(np.float32)-18,0,255)).astype(np.uint8)
    budget_views.append(view)
    selected_records.append([operation_names[i] for i in selected])
fig = panels(budget_views,[f"Budget {n}: {', '.join(names) or 'identity'}" for n,names in zip([0,1,2],selected_records)])

Read the result

Each title records what actually happened. Sampling without replacement avoids applying the same selected operation twice, while sorting defines a stable order. Budget limits are a review tool, not a guarantee that every sampled image is useful.

Change and compare

  • Use the same selected record to replay a view on another training mug.
  • Compare a count budget with separately bounding angle and brightness magnitude.

Guided task 04

Auditing Sampled Distributions

Inspect more than a few attractive examples when reviewing a random policy. Record many draws and compare their observed ranges and application frequencies with the configured bounds. A histogram reveals the implemented sampling distribution; it does not prove that the distribution matches a real deployment environment. Here angle is uniform from −8 to 8 degrees, brightness is uniform from −12 to 12, and reflection is an independent probability-0.3 decision.

Use the same stored row to construct a displayed example. That links a visible image to the numeric audit instead of presenting an unrelated illustration. Small samples vary, and finite histograms need not be perfectly flat. Check impossible values and implementation mistakes first. Later, domain evidence can justify narrower or different distributions; do not infer appropriate severity solely from the fact that random draws appear well distributed.

Try it

  1. Draw 300 parameter records with seed 1014.
  2. Inspect angle, offset and flip frequency.
  3. Apply the first recorded parameters to the mug.
Python · run in order
audit_rng = np.random.default_rng(1014)
angles = audit_rng.uniform(-8,8,300)
offsets = audit_rng.uniform(-12,12,300)
flips = audit_rng.random(300) < .3
audit_base = image[:,::-1].copy() if flips[0] else image.copy()
audit_affine = cv2.getRotationMatrix2D(((w-1)/2,(h-1)/2),float(angles[0]),1)
audit_view = cv2.warpAffine(audit_base,audit_affine,(w,h),borderValue=(225,218,200))
audit_view = np.rint(np.clip(audit_view.astype(np.float32)+offsets[0],0,255)).astype(np.uint8)
fig,axes = plt.subplots(1,3,figsize=(12,3.5))
axes[0].imshow(audit_view)
axes[0].set_title(f"First draw; flip={bool(flips[0])}")
axes[0].axis("off")
axes[1].hist(angles,bins=12,range=(-8,8))
axes[1].set(xlabel="Angle (degrees)",ylabel="Count",title="300 sampled angles")
axes[2].hist(offsets,bins=12,range=(-12,12))
axes[2].set(xlabel="Brightness offset",ylabel="Count",title=f"Flip frequency: {flips.mean():.1%}")
fig.tight_layout()

Read the result

The histograms are measurements of these 300 records. They can expose an excluded endpoint mistake, a wrong unit or an unintended bias, but they cannot establish an accuracy benefit without a later controlled model experiment.

Change and compare

  • Replay the first record after drawing more random numbers.
  • Reduce the sample count to ten and compare how uneven the histograms become.

Guided task 05

MixUp Images and Soft Targets

MixUp combines two classification examples by a convex weighted average. Convert both RGB arrays to float32 [0,1], then form lambda×A+(1−lambda)×B with lambda between zero and one. Blend their one-hot targets with the same weight. Our class order is [mug,apple], so the target is a two-element vector rather than one unchanged integer class ID.

The mixed picture is intentionally not a natural photograph of one object. Its soft target describes the training construction, not a measured probability that a physical scene contains a mug. This method is an optional classification training technique to evaluate later, not a generic preprocessing rule for every task. Pixelwise segmentation masks cannot be replaced by the same two-class image-level target. Only pair examples from the training split, and keep original labels available for audit.

Try it

  1. Create float mug and apple images.
  2. Blend pixels using lambda 0.65.
  3. Blend one-hot targets using exactly the same lambda.
Python · run in order
a = scene("mug").astype(np.float32)/255.0
b = scene("apple").astype(np.float32)/255.0
target_a = np.array([1.,0.],np.float32)
target_b = np.array([0.,1.],np.float32)
lam = .65
mixed = lam*a + (1-lam)*b
soft_target = lam*target_a + (1-lam)*target_b
fig = panels([a,b,mixed], ["Mug target [1,0]","Apple target [0,1]",f"MixUp target {soft_target.round(2)}"])

Read the result

The overlapping outlines make the artificial construction visible. The target sums to one and matches the image weights. Retaining only the mug label would discard how the second training example contributed to the mixed input.

Change and compare

  • Set lambda to zero and one and verify both endpoint images and targets.
  • Mix two mug examples and explain why their soft target remains [1,0].

Guided task 06

CutMix and Actual Clipped Area

CutMix replaces a rectangle from a base classification image with pixels from a donor image of the same size. The target weights follow the fraction of the output canvas actually pasted. A proposed rectangle may extend outside the image, so compute its clipped integer bounds before calculating area. Using the requested rectangle size or a pre-clipping lambda creates a mismatch between image construction and target weights.

Our proposed rectangle is x=−12:70 and y=40:112 on a 160-by-128 canvas. Clip x to 0:70; the pasted area is 70×72 pixels. The base weight is one minus that area divided by the canvas area. Copy matching donor coordinates into that region. Area weighting describes the technique, not the true fraction of visible object evidence; a pasted patch might contain mostly table. This is again classification mixing, not a universal segmentation transformation.

Try it

  1. Clip the proposed rectangle to the canvas.
  2. Paste donor pixels into a copy of the base.
  3. Compute the target from actual clipped area.
Python · run in order
requested = (-12,40,70,112)
x1,y1,x2,y2 = requested
x1,x2 = np.clip([x1,x2],0,w).astype(int)
y1,y2 = np.clip([y1,y2],0,h).astype(int)
pasted_area = max(0,x2-x1)*max(0,y2-y1)
base_weight = 1-pasted_area/(h*w)
cutmix = a.copy()
cutmix[y1:y2,x1:x2] = b[y1:y2,x1:x2]
cut_target = base_weight*target_a+(1-base_weight)*target_b
fig = panels([a,b,cutmix], ["Base mug","Donor apple",f"CutMix base weight {base_weight:.4f}"])

Read the result

The pasted rectangle has a sharp geometric boundary because this method replaces a region instead of blending each pixel. Its actual area determines the target, even when the originally requested rectangle crossed the image border.

Change and compare

  • Move the requested rectangle fully outside the canvas and derive the identity result.
  • Paste a full-canvas rectangle and verify the target becomes the donor target.

Guided task 07

Batch Pairing and Target Bookkeeping

Mixing a batch requires keeping the image pairing and label pairing identical. An index array identifies the donor for each base example. Apply that same array to the target matrix. A common bug shuffles images but leaves targets in their original order, producing numerically valid soft vectors that describe the wrong pair.

This four-example batch alternates mug and apple drawings and uses a one-position cyclic donor shift. The lambda array contains a separate weight for each base example; reshape it to N,1,1,1 for image broadcasting and N,1 for target broadcasting. The shape changes express different tensor roles, not different weights. Record original indices, donor indices and lambda values if a mixed sample needs to be reconstructed. Keep the entire construction within training data and never use held-out images as convenient donors.

Try it

  1. Stack four independently drawn training examples.
  2. Create one donor index array for both images and targets.
  3. Broadcast the same lambda values over pixels and class coordinates.
Python · run in order
kinds = ["mug","apple","mug","apple"]
batch = np.stack([scene(kind,seed=i).astype(np.float32)/255 for i,kind in enumerate(kinds)])
labels = np.array([0,1,0,1])
targets = np.eye(2,dtype=np.float32)[labels]
donors = np.roll(np.arange(4),1)
weights = np.array([.2,.4,.6,.8],np.float32)
mixed_batch = weights[:,None,None,None]*batch+(1-weights[:,None,None,None])*batch[donors]
mixed_targets = weights[:,None]*targets+(1-weights[:,None])*targets[donors]
fig = panels(list(mixed_batch),[f"Base {i}, donor {donors[i]}\ntarget {mixed_targets[i].round(2)}" for i in range(4)])

Read the result

Every title identifies its pair and target. Image and target arrays need different broadcasting dimensions, but their leading example axis must remain aligned. A valid sum of one alone cannot prove that each target describes the correct donor.

Change and compare

  • Swap only the donor targets to construct a detectable bookkeeping fault.
  • Use all weights equal to one and verify the unmodified batch and original targets.

Guided task 08

Controlled Policy Comparison Plans

A policy audit can prepare a later experiment without training a model now. Define a baseline and a small set of alternatives that differ in one documented component: geometry only, appearance only, and their composition. Hold the raw training groups, validation groups, deterministic evaluation path and future training budget fixed. Otherwise a measured difference could come from a changed split or procedure rather than the augmentation under study.

Display the same source under all four conditions to verify that the implementation matches the plan. Record array checks and policy settings now; leave model metrics explicitly unmeasured. If a later validation experiment selects a policy, train with that selected augmentation and evaluate the resulting model once on the untouched test set using fixed deterministic preprocessing, with no stochastic test augmentation. More attractive previews, wider input variation or lower reconstruction error do not by themselves establish a recognition benefit.

Try it

  1. Construct baseline, geometry, appearance and combined previews.
  2. Store the planned conditions as plain data.
  3. Check fixed output dimensions without assigning accuracy scores.
Python · run in order
geo_matrix = np.float32([[1,0,6],[0,1,-3]])
geometry = cv2.warpAffine(image,geo_matrix,(w,h),borderValue=(225,218,200))
appearance = np.rint(np.clip(image.astype(np.float32)-12,0,255)).astype(np.uint8)
both = np.rint(np.clip(geometry.astype(np.float32)-12,0,255)).astype(np.uint8)
conditions = [{"name":"baseline","geometry":False,"appearance":False},{"name":"geometry","geometry":True,"appearance":False},{"name":"appearance","geometry":False,"appearance":True},{"name":"combined","geometry":True,"appearance":True}]
comparison_plan = {"conditions":conditions,"fixed":["group split","evaluation preprocessing","future model and training budget"],"model_metrics":"not measured"}
fig = panels([image,geometry,appearance,both],[x["name"] for x in conditions])

Read the result

The pictures verify policy mechanics and common array contracts. The stored plan deliberately contains no invented accuracy values. A future comparison needs repeated, controlled measurements and uncertainty appropriate to its data and training procedure.

Change and compare

  • Add a no-mixing versus MixUp comparison while keeping the donor pool training-only.
  • Specify which validation criterion would select a policy before measuring any results.
